title: The Microeconomics of Cloud Hyperscalers
excerpt: Deconstructing modern hyperscale economics: GPU depreciation cycles, nuclear power purchase agreements, and the capital expenditure moat of artificial intelligence.
author: Claire Dupont

body.text: The Industrial Transformation of Modern Computing

Cloud computing has completed its transition from an operational expense (OpEx) utility model into the most capital-intensive infrastructure buildout in modern industrial history. Leading hyperscalers now deploy tens of billions of dollars quarterly into physical real estate, high-voltage electrical interconnects, liquid-cooled server racks, and specialized semiconductor accelerators.
The Core Economic Drivers of Hyperscale Dominance

body.alt: Interconnect networking architecture and infrastructure topology in enterprise data centers
body.caption: Capital expenditure: Giant amortized server clusters create insurmountable cost advantages against private on-premise infrastructure.

items: Accelerated Depreciation Schedules: Hyperscalers amortize general-purpose servers over 4 to 6 years, but AI accelerators (GPUs/TPUs) face compressed 3-year cycles due to rapid generational obsolescence.
Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs): Securing gigawatt-scale, 20-year baseload contracts with nuclear and geothermal utilities to ensure uninterrupted power independent of grid volatility.
Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE): Custom closed-loop liquid cooling and direct-to-chip cold plates drive hyperscale PUE below 1.15, compared to 1.50+ for legacy enterprise data centers.
Dark Fiber & Subsea Corridors: Hyperscale-owned trans-oceanic fiber optic links eliminate transit fees and deliver sub-millisecond interconnect bandwidth between regional availability zones.

body.text: In the artificial intelligence era, the competitive moat is no longer software; it is gigawatts of connected baseload power and hundred-billion-dollar balance sheet capacity.
body.cite: Claire Dupont, Hyperscale Capital & Corporate Strategy

body.text: The Power Wall: Electrical Grid Constraints and Dedicated Generation

The primary bottleneck limiting data center expansion is no longer silicon availability, but electrical interconnection queues. With regional transmission operators projecting decade-long delays for high-capacity grid connections, hyperscalers are co-locating data campuses directly behind the meter at nuclear power plants or financing dedicated small modular reactor (SMR) deployments.

body.text: Capital Intensity and the Creation of Permanent Oligopolies

The astronomical capital requirement to train frontier models and serve inference at global scale is creating an insurmountable economic barrier to entry. As software startups face surging compute costs, value accrues disproportionately to infrastructure landlords who monetize land, power, and amortized silicon through programmatic cloud APIs.
